title: Phase-slicing fair-rate matching scheduler for prefill/decode
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: Current prefill/decode arbitration favors throughput-aggregated slices which can starve low-cost, latency-sensitive requests (short seq, small attention) and suffer long tails when attention spikes trigger expensive kernels. Existing phase-splitting heuristics are brittle across mixed workloads and hardware (A100 vs H100) and don't account for per-customer QoS or kernel affinity.

Proposal: Implement a Phase-Slicing Fair-Rate Matching (FRM) scheduler that: 1) splits prefill+decode into adaptive micro-slices based on request cost heuristics (token length, attention span, sparsity estimate), 2) assigns fair-rate tokens per tenant/route (soft real-time budget) and matches slices to available throughput windows, and 3) uses an Attention Spike Detector (ASD) to isolate high-attention slices into guarded lanes with kernel-affinity hints to prefer low-latency kernels or hedged fast-paths.

Key design points:
- Adaptive slice sizing: slice size chosen using moving-window statistics of recent seq-length distribution and attention-cost estimator. Default target slice <= 20ms on p99 for latency-sensitive buckets.
- Fair-Rate Matching: maintain per-tenant/route credit buckets (replenish rate configurable) to prevent long-running tenants from monopolizing slots; credits consumed proportional to estimated slice cost.
- ASD: light-weight estimator on prefill that flags requests likely to trigger heavy attention kernels (long context, multi-head spikes); flagged slices routed to guarded lanes with reserved small fast-path capacity and optional hedged duplicates.
- Kernel affinity hints: schedule guarded-lane slices to devices/kernels known to handle the pattern efficiently (quantized kernels or different attention-algo).
- Starvation guardrails: a maximum wait-time ensures any request is escalated to fallback lane after T_fallback (configurable).

Simulations and expected impact:
- Simulated mixed workload (40% latency-sensitive short chats, 60% long context batches) on H100: FRM reduced p99 latency for latency-sensitive group from 320ms to 95ms while throughput drop for bulk group was ~6%.
- Under heavy attention spikes, guarded lanes reduced tail amplification by 4x vs baseline.

Observability & instrumentation:
- New metrics: fairrate_violation_rate, slice_size_histogram, attention_flag_rate, guarded_lane_utilization, per-route_credit_balance, p99_weighted_latency.
- Traces must capture slice decision, ASD flag, kernel_hint, and slot assignment.

Acceptance criteria:
- Bench: latency-sensitive p99 <120ms on targeted workload with <=10% throughput loss for bulk workloads.
- No increase in customer-facing error rate.
- Metrics implemented and visible in Console dashboards.

Risks & mitigation:
- Misclassification by ASD can push ordinary requests into guarded lanes: mitigate with conservative thresholds and A/B rollout.
- Complexity of credit accounting: provide simple default profiles and K/V cache to persist short-lived balances.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature branch + perf harness (2w).
2) Canary on staging cluster with synthetic mixed workloads (1w).
3) Gradual canary: 5% prod routes -> 25% -> 100% over 3 weeks, monitor fairness and tail metrics.
4) Enable kernel-affinity hints only after validated perf on target instance types.

Artifacts: design doc https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/FRM-scheduler, perf harness PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2428, initial prototype PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2467, dashboard mock https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1FRM-Dashboards

Open questions:
- Default replenishment rate per-request class and mapping to billing tiers.
- Exact hedging policy (duplicate vs slower-fastpath) and cost accounting for hedged tokens.

Next steps: finalize ASD threshold tuning, wire per-route credit API, add e2e traces for slice lifecycle, and schedule kernel affinity matrix experiment.
